are three notational systems: 1. level notation 2. composite notation 3. matrix notation ... which is consistent with what I'm seeing in this other paper. There is also [this source](https://datalorax.github.io/equatiomatic/) which is about turning formula into latex equations. ## Level Notation - Introduced by Bryk and Raudenbush 1992 - formulate a multilevel model as a **system of two equations**, one at level-1, and two at level-2: (Here I am substituting all the $c$s with all the $j$s in the original system) $$\begin{align} \texttt{lpo}_{ij} &= \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1j}\texttt{sex}_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij} \\ \beta_{0j} &= \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01} \texttt{den}_j + u_{0j} \\ \beta_{1j} &= \gamma_{10} \end{align} $$ where $\texttt{lpo}_{ij}$ is the test score of pupile $i$ in school $j$. Note here that the subscripts distinguish the level-1 and level-2 variables. ## Composite Notation We can also substitute the level-2 models into level-1 model and result in the following single predictive equation: $$ \texttt{lpo}_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{sex}_{ij} + \beta_2 \texttt{den}_j + u_{0j} + \epsilon_{ij} $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m1 <- lmer(lpo ~ 1 + sex + den + (1 | sch), data = df) m1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] Formula: lpo ~ 1 + sex + den + (1 | sch) Data: df REML criterion at convergence: 25717.17 Random effects: Groups Name Std.Dev. sch (Intercept) 3.962 Residual 7.858 Number of obs: 3648, groups: sch, 198 Fixed Effects: (Intercept) sex1 den2 den3 den4 38.068 2.273 3.276 1.143 4.593 ``` ::: ::: We can also use the equatiomatic package to double check: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} extract_eq(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{lpo}_{i} &\sim N \left(\alpha_{j[i]} + \beta_{1}(\operatorname{sex}_{\operatorname{1}}), \sigma^2 \right) \\ \alpha_{j} &\sim N \left(\gamma_{0}^{\alpha} + \gamma_{1}^{\alpha}(\operatorname{den}_{\operatorname{2}}) + \gamma_{2}^{\alpha}(\operatorname{den}_{\operatorname{3}}) + \gamma_{3}^{\alpha}(\operatorname{den}_{\operatorname{4}}), \sigma^2_{\alpha_{j}} \right) \text{, for sch j = 1,} \dots \text{,J} \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: And the version with the actual coefficient: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} extract_eq(m1, use_coefs = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{\widehat{lpo}}_{i} &\sim N \left(38.07_{\alpha_{j[i]}} + 2.27_{\beta_{1}}(\operatorname{sex}_{\operatorname{1}}), \sigma^2 \right) \\ \alpha_{j} &\sim N \left(3.28_{\gamma_{1}^{\alpha}}(\operatorname{den}_{\operatorname{2}}) + 1.14_{\gamma_{2}^{\alpha}}(\operatorname{den}_{\operatorname{3}}) + 4.59_{\gamma_{3}^{\alpha}}(\operatorname{den}_{\operatorname{4}}), 3.96 \right) \text{, for sch j = 1,} \dots \text{,J} \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: ## Matrix Notation Still the same model can be written in matrix notation as $$ y_j = X_j \beta + Z_j u_j + \epsilon_j $$ where $y_j = \texttt{lpo}_j$ is a column vector containing the scores in cluster $j$, where $X_j = (1, \texttt{den}_j, \texttt{sec}_j)$ is the design matrix, a ## Domains and preferences - The matrix model formulation is favoured among statisticians^[for example, [this blog posts](https://stats.oarc.ucla.edu/other/mult-pkg/introduction-to-linear-mixed-models/) uses the matrix notation] - The level notation is common in the social sciences, as they separate the roles of level-1 and level-2 variables, which eases interpretation of the model and error structures - The composite formulation covers the middle ground, for its balance between compactness and clarity, and is used by the introductions into the multilevel analysis for applied researchers - I think the Bayesian wind is most similar to this --- ## Which of these map best to `lme4` and `brms` syntax? The composite notation maps best to `lme4` and `brms` syntax. What about the syntax? Xiaoying provides some lead here but it's like Wilkinson-Rogers -> Wilkinson-Rogers-Pinheiro-Bates (`lm(y ~ x + z)`) and then Paurl Burkner for the brms syntax (`response | aterms ~ pterms + (gterms | group)`). :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## What's up with all this terminology? My mental model of how hierarchical models work is heavily influenced by @mcelreath2020statistical. In his book, McElreath said: > I adopt the terminology of @gelman2005analysis, who argues that the common term *random effects* hardly aids with understanding, for most people. Indeed, it seems to encourage misunderstanding, partly because the terms *fixed* and *random effects* mean different things to different statisticians. See pages 20--21 of Gelman's paper. I fully realize, however, that by trying to spread Gelman's alternative jargon, I am essentially splitting into a very strong wind. The TLDR is that there have been a lot of different definitions of fixed and random effects in different contexts, across different disciplines. Gelman chose to sidestep the overloaded terms and define > ... effects (or coefficients) in a multilevel model as *constant* if they are identical for all groups in a population and *varying* if they are allowed to differ from group to group. What this implies in terms of how the math notation^[Referring to section 12.1 Notation from @gelman2007data] is that - Units $i = 1, ..., n$ - Outcome measurements $y = (y_1, ..., y_n)$ - Regression predictors represented by an $n \times k$ matrix $X$ - Groups $j = 1, ..., J$. This works for a single level of grouping (e.g., students within schools, persons within states, tadpoles within tanks) - Occasioally use $k = 1, ..., K$ for a second level of grouping (e.g., students within schools within districts) - Index variable $j[i]$ code group membership. For example, if you get $j[35] = 4$ that means the 35th data unit in the data belongs to group 4. ::: # Notation type 1. Composite --- "composite form" see Singer 1998 - "essentially the presentation used for mixed effects models" - $\beta$ represent the average effects of variables that are known as *fixed effects* - $u$ represents heterogeneity between the groups, typically called *random effects* - closer in structure to the syntax used in SAS, STATA, and R (`nlme`, `lmer`) 2. Level - Bayesian models "naturally related terms through hierarchical structures" 3. Matrix - the best way to express something succinctly - $\mathbf{y} = X \mathbf{\beta} + Z \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{\epsilon}$ - ... where $X_j$ is the **design matrix** for the fixed effects and $Z_j$ is the design matrix for the **random effects**. ## Math notation and design formula According to @mcelreath2020statistical, it is a compact form of notation, that are intimately related to a "common matrix algebra description of linear models". If you've run `lmer` code before you know what something like `y ~ 1 + x` means. [Xiaoying Pu](https://xiaoyingpu.github.io/) provided a [cheat sheet](https://xiaoyingpu.github.io/note/cheat/) for reading/writing R formulas used in `lmer` and `brms`. In @barrRandomEffectsStructure2013, the provide a nice table. In @gaSoftwareFittingMultilevel2013, they looked at the software for fitting multilevel models, and they had a nice table^[Table 26.1] about statistical software packages containing modules/functions designed to fix various classes of mixed-effects models. Below I will reproduce this table, but focusing only on the `R` side of things: | `R` package | Linear Mixed Models
**LMM** | Generalized Linear Mixed Models
**GLMM** | Nonlinear Mixed Models
**NLMM** | |---------|:-----|------:|:------:| | [`nlme`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nlme/index.html) | 12 | 12 | 12 | | [`lme4`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lme4/index.html) | 123 | 123 | 123 | | [`brms`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/brms/index.html) | 1 | 1 | 1 | : `R` software packages and functions for fitting mixed models. --- We will leverage this paper^[Multilevel Model Notation - Establishing the commonalities] but use the dataset (`brandsma` object in the `mice` package) mentioned by this source^[https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-threeformulations.html]. We will concentrate on four variables: - `sch`: school number - `lpo`: language test post, outcome at pupil level. - `sex`: sex of pupil - `den`: school denomination, predictor at school level. ## Some preliminary checks ::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} df %>% ggplot(aes(x = lpo, color = sex)) + geom_density() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} df %>% ggplot(aes(x = lpo, color = den)) + geom_density() + facet_wrap(~sex) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-2.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Unconditional Means model $$y_{ij} = \beta_0 + u_{0j} + \epsilon_{ij}$$ The model posits that the score of a randomly selected student $i$ in a randomly selected school $j$ can be represented as a sum of: - the population mean $\beta_0$ - the effect of being in school $j$: $u_{0j}$ - the effect of being a particular student in school $j$: $\epsilon_{ij}$ `TODO`: I don't think the following is correct ... ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # lmer(lpo ~ 1 + den + (1 | den), data = df) ``` ::: ## Composite Notation The same model can be rewritten as $$\texttt{lpo}_{ic}=\beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{sex}_{ic} + \beta_2 \texttt{den}_c + u_{0c} + \epsilon_{ic}$$ Which in Gelman notation, is something like (`TODO` this is not right ...) $$\texttt{lpo}_{i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{sex}_{\texttt{class}[i]} + \beta_2 \texttt{den}_{j[i]} + u_{0c} + \epsilon_{ic} $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # lmer(lpo ~ 1 + sex + den + (1 | 1 + sex + den), data = df) ``` ::: --- > Multilevel models contain two forms of stochastic variation, usually called variance components, captured in random effects $u_{0j}$ and error $\epsilon_{ij}$ terms,
